# Problem 1
```{r p1_cleaning}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa = ny_noaa |> 
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month"), 4) |> 
  separate(month, into= c("month", "day"), 3) |> 
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    month = as.numeric(month)*-1,
    day = as.numeric(day)*-1,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax),
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)
  )

#According to the codebook, precipitation is reported in tenths of mm, so we need to divide by 10; tmax and tmin are also in tenths of degrees C

ny_noaa = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp/10,
    tmax = tmax/10,
    tmin = tmin/10
  )
```

This dataset contains daily weather data for New York from `r min(pull(ny_noaa, year))` to `r max(pull(ny_noaa, year))`. The variables include the date, maximum and minimum temperatures, precipitation, and snowfall. There are `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations in this dataset. The average values for each variable are as follows:
- the average maximum temperature is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, tmax), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` degrees Celsius
- the average minimum temperature is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, tmin), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` degrees Celsius
- the average precipitation is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, prcp), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm
- the average snowfall is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, snow), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm
- the average snowfall depth is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, snwd), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm

There is quite a bit of missing data in this dataset. There are,
- `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax)))` missing values for maximum temperature (`r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100` % of the data)
- `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin)))` missing values for minimum temperature (`r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100` % of the data)
- `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp)))` missing values for precipitation (`r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100` % of the data)
- `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow)))` missing values for snowfall (`r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100` % of the data)


```{r snow_hist}
ny_noaa |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow)) + 
  geom_histogram()
```

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```
The most commonly observed values are close to 0 for snowfall. Specifically, the most common values (aside from NA) are 0, 25, and 13 mm. This is because this weather data is taken for every day of the year, and in NY, there is only snow a couple months of the year, and there only tends to be a couple of days of heavy snowfall a year.

```{r june_july_maxtemp}
ny_noaa |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |> 
  mutate(
    month = case_match(
      month,
      1 ~ "January",
      7 ~ "July"
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  mutate(avg_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = avg_tmax)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth()+
  facet_grid(.~month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temperature (C)"
  )
```
The values appear to be much lower in January than July. They also tend to be more variable in January. There appears to be one outlier in July (with a couple other points being potential outliers). It is hard to tell if any of the January values would be considered outliers without conducting further analyses. The graphs show a cyclical pattern rather than a long-term change over time, consistent with what we would expect for weather from year to year.

Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); and (ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r tmax_min_plot}
p1_i_plot = ny_noaa |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  labs(
    x = "Minimum Temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (C)"
  )

p1_ii_plot = ny_noaa |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) + 
  geom_density_ridges() + 
  labs(x = "Snowfall (mm)", y = "Year")

p1_i_plot + p1_ii_plot
```

There appears to be a strong linear trend between maximum and minimum temperatures. There appears to be a few stations for which tmax is reported as lower than tmin, so there are errors in the data. There are also some extreme values (i.e. 60 degrees C) that are not plausible for NY.

Additionally, each year shows higher counts of lower snowfall amounts. In most years, there appear to be a couple days with bigger snowfalls (around 80mm), which are likely from the 1-2 storms we have each year. Otherwise, most snowfall clusters between 0-40mm. 

# Problem 2
```{r p2_data}
# for nhanes_demog, 1 = male, 2 = female, 1 = Less than high school, 2 =  High school equivalent, 3  = More than high school

nhanes_demog = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female"
    ),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
      )
    ) |> 
  mutate(
    education = fct_relevel(education, c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")),
    sex = fct_relevel(sex, c("Male", "Female"))
  ) |> 
  filter(age > 21) |> 
  drop_na()

nhanes_accel = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

nhanes = left_join(nhanes_demog, nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")
```

```{r sex_ed_tbl}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |> 
  summarize(
    count=n()
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
```

```{r sex_ed_age_plot}
nhanes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=sex, y = age))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  facet_grid(.~education)
```
The distributions of all of the groups overlap substantially. In general, people with more than high school educations are a bit younger, though the quantiles overlap substantially. 

```{r}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, education) |> 
  mutate(
    total_mims = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_mims, color = sex))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth()+
  facet_grid(.~education)+
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total Activity (MIMS)"
  )
```

Total activity tends to trend downward with age in all groups. Additionally, the "Less than high school" has a steeper downward trend than the other two groups. Generally, males and females follow the same pattern in all three education groups. The trend does appear to be more defined in "Less than high school" than the other two groups.

```{r}
nhanes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mims, color = sex)) + 
 #geom_point(alpha = 0.1) + I cant decide if I like the points (leaning no)
  geom_smooth() + 
  facet_grid(.~education)
```

In all three graphs, activity happens in the middle of the day. Females have slightly higher activity than males. There does not appear to be any major differences activity across education groups. Where "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" tend to plateau through the day, "less than high school" has more of a point around minute 750.

# Problem 3
```{r}
citibike_0120 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |> 
  mutate(month = "Jan",
         year = "2020")
citibike_0720 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv")|> 
  mutate(month = "July",
         year = "2020")
citibike_0124 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")|> 
  mutate(month = "Jan",
         year = "2024")
citibike_0724 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv")|> 
  mutate(month = "July",
         year = "2024")

citibike = bind_rows(citibike_0120, citibike_0720, citibike_0124, citibike_0724) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    month = fct_relevel(month, c("Jan", "July")),
    year = fct_relevel(year, c("2020", "2024")),
    rideable_type = fct_relevel(rideable_type, c("classic_bike", "docked_bike", "electric_bike")),
    weekdays = fct_relevel(weekdays, c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"))
  )
  
citibike |> 
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |> 
  summarize(
    total_rides = n()
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = total_rides
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
```
From this table, it is evident that both members and casual riders tend to ride more in July than January. Additionally, across both casual riders and members, rides increased between 2020 and 2024. Overall, there are more members than casual riders across all groups.


```{r}
citibike |> 
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July") |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(
    total_rides = n()
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(total_rides)) |>
  head(n=5) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
```

```{r}
citibike |> 
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |> 
  summarize(
    median_ride_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_ride_duration, color = month, group = month)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_grid(.~year) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
```

From these plots, it is evident that the median ride duration is longer in July than January in both 2020 and 2024. Additionally, the median ride duration is longer in 2020 than 2024. In July of both years, the median ride duration tends to be longest on weekends and shortest on weekdays. In January, though, in 2020 the median ride duration is higher on weekends, but in 2024, it is relatively constant, with the longest median ride duration of Thursday-Saturday. 

There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.
```{r}
citibike |> 
  filter(year == "2024") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, y = rideable_type, fill = member_casual)) + 
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_grid(.~month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Bike Type"
  )
```
According to the above graphs, electric bike usage tends to be a bit higher in January than July for both casual riders and members. Additionally, across all graphs, there is a much higher density of shorter rides (less than 45 minutes) than longer rides. The distribution of ride duration is similar across casual riders and members, though casual riders tend to have a slightly higher density of longer rides than members.
